audit.costConcern: 740 is 1.00x the A2 civics median (740); within range.
audit.rationale: Sound root of the legitimacy lane with six dependents; the OR of the two surplus economies is historically right.

newNodes.name: Burial of the dead
newNodes.emerged: ~100 kya Qafzeh and Skhul burials with ochre; ~34 kya Sungir grave goods
newNodes.prereqRationale: ochre_processing: the oldest burials (Qafzeh) are ochre-stained; ochre is dated ~100 kya, as early as the burials.
newNodes.rationale: ochre_processing: the oldest burials (Qafzeh) are ochre-stained; ochre is dated ~100 kya, as early as the burials.
newNodes.desc: The band buries its dead with ochre and ornaments and mourns them together, binding the living to one another and to the places where their kin lie.
newNodes.effectRationale: Shared mourning rites absorb the strain a death puts on a small band, so grievance builds more slowly.
newNodes.distinctFrom: shamanic_ritual is a specialist's role; burial is a community-wide rite needing no specialist. ancestor_veneration (A2) is the later settled cult of named ancestors.

newNodes.name: Sacred gathering places
newNodes.emerged: ~17 kya Lascaux; ~15 kya Altamira (reading painted caves as band-aggregation sites is an archaeological inference)
newNodes.prereqRationale: shamanic_ritual: the rites performed at the shared place are led by ritual specialists (dated from ~35 kya).
newNodes.rationale: shamanic_ritual: the rites performed at the shared place are led by ritual specialists (dated from ~35 kya).
newNodes.desc: Bands that live apart meet at painted caves and shrines in certain seasons to hold rites, exchange news and find spouses.
newNodes.effectRationale: Seasonal aggregation keeps distant bands in contact and marrying between groups, so people move further between them.
newNodes.distinctFrom: shamanic_ritual is who leads the rite; this is where scattered bands gather for it.

newNodes.name: Prestige leadership
newNodes.emerged: ~10 kya and earlier: ethnographic headmen whose influence rests on generosity and skill (inferred for late foragers)
newNodes.prereqRationale: gift_exchange: a headman's standing comes from giving. kin_council: he leads by persuading the council of household heads. Both are A1.
newNodes.rationale: gift_exchange: a headman's standing comes from giving. kin_council: he leads by persuading the council of household heads. Both are A1.
newNodes.desc: Some men and women lead by skill and generosity rather than birth: others follow them on the hunt, in moves and in disputes, but can leave them at will.
newNodes.effectRationale: A respected leader can draw a larger following when a group splits to found a new camp, so founding parties are larger.
newNodes.distinctFrom: kin_council is collective deliberation; this is personal, achieved authority within it. hereditary_rank (A2) is authority by birth.

newNodes.name: Monumental shrines
newNodes.emerged: ~9,500 BCE Göbekli Tepe enclosures; ~3,000 BCE Stonehenge
newNodes.prereqRationale: communal_feasts: Göbekli Tepe's builders were fed at great feasts (~9,500 BCE, same date). shamanic_ritual: the enclosures are ritual spaces.
newNodes.rationale: communal_feasts: Göbekli Tepe's builders were fed at great feasts (~9,500 BCE, same date). shamanic_ritual: the enclosures are ritual spaces.
newNodes.desc: Communities raise stone enclosures and tombs too large for any household, feeding the work parties with feasts and gathering at them for rites.
newNodes.effectRationale: Organizing many households into fed work parties is the first mass labour mobilization; the same practice serves later communal works such as tracks and causeways.
newNodes.distinctFrom: communal_feasts is the feast; this is the monument the feast pays for. corvee_labour (A3) is labour owed to a state, not volunteered to a shrine.

newNodes.name: Insignia of rank
newNodes.emerged: ~4,500 BCE Varna gold sceptre and ornaments; ~3,500 BCE Nahal Mishmar copper maceheads
newNodes.prereqRationale: hereditary_rank: insignia mark inherited office (Varna, ~4,500 BCE, same date). copper_native OR gold_silver_native: the earliest regalia are of native copper and gold.
newNodes.rationale: hereditary_rank: insignia mark inherited office (Varna, ~4,500 BCE, same date). copper_native OR gold_silver_native: the earliest regalia are of native copper and gold.
newNodes.desc: Sceptres, maces and gold ornaments mark who holds rank, so authority is recognized by people who have never met its holder.
newNodes.effectRationale: A recognizable emblem lets a leader's word carry to villages beyond personal acquaintance, so authority reaches further.
newNodes.distinctFrom: hereditary_rank is the rule of inheritance; regalia are its visible signs, which carry authority beyond face-to-face contact.

newNodes.name: First-comer precedence
newNodes.emerged: ~7,000 BCE Çatalhöyük house continuity over many generations (inferred); ethnographic earth-priest lineages of West Africa
newNodes.prereqRationale: ancestor_veneration: precedence is claimed through the ancestors who first cleared the land (dated ~9,000 BCE).
newNodes.rationale: ancestor_veneration: precedence is claimed through the ancestors who first cleared the land (dated ~9,000 BCE).
newNodes.desc: The lineage descended from the first settlers keeps the shrine of the land and allots fields to later arrivals, who farm by its leave.
newNodes.effectRationale: A recognized founding lineage can allot outlying land to newcomers, so a settlement draws on a wider hinterland.
newNodes.distinctFrom: ancestor_veneration honours the dead; this turns descent from the first settlers into a claim over land and newcomers.

newNodes.name: Segmentary lineage society
newNodes.emerged: ~6,000 BCE Neolithic lineage villages (inferred); ethnographic Nuer and Tiv
newNodes.prereqRationale: ancestor_veneration: lineages are defined by a common ancestor. kin_council: each segment is run by its elders. Both precede the node.
newNodes.rationale: ancestor_veneration: lineages are defined by a common ancestor. kin_council: each segment is run by its elders. Both precede the node.
newNodes.desc: Lineages unite against outsiders and split when they grow, with no permanent chief; elders of each segment settle disputes.
newNodes.effectRationale: Segments bud off and move away as they grow, so people move more freely.
newNodes.distinctFrom: chiefdom has a permanent paramount; tribal_confederacy is a sworn league. This form has neither: unity by descent, fission by growth.

newNodes.name: Big-man polity
newNodes.emerged: ~6,500 BCE early Neolithic villages (inferred from feasting debris); ethnographic Melanesian big-men
newNodes.prereqRationale: prestige_leadership: the big-man is the achieved leader. communal_feasts: he wins followers by competitive feasting. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: prestige_leadership: the big-man is the achieved leader. communal_feasts: he wins followers by competitive feasting. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: Leaders compete for followers by sponsoring feasts and exchanges; their authority lasts only as long as their generosity and is not inherited.
newNodes.effectRationale: Households work harder to produce surplus for their leader's feasts (Sahlins), so each farmer produces more.
newNodes.distinctFrom: chiefdom is hereditary office; the big-man's position is achieved and lapses with him.

newNodes.name: Enthronement rites
newNodes.emerged: ~3,000 BCE Egyptian accession rites (union of the Two Lands); ~1,000 BCE Babylonian re-investiture at the Akitu festival
newNodes.prereqRationale: sacral_kingship: enthronement is the rite that makes a man the god-sanctioned king (dated ~3,100 BCE).
newNodes.rationale: sacral_kingship: enthronement is the rite that makes a man the god-sanctioned king (dated ~3,100 BCE).
newNodes.desc: A new ruler is installed by public rite: anointing, crowning and the oath of the great men, so everyone knows who rules from the day of accession.
newNodes.effectRationale: Governors and vassals swear at the enthronement, so the new ruler's authority is recognized in the provinces at once.
newNodes.distinctFrom: succession_law says who the heir is; this rite makes the accession public and binding.

newNodes.name: State pantheon
newNodes.emerged: ~2,600 BCE Fara god lists; ~2,100 BCE Nippur as the seat of Enlil, who confers kingship
newNodes.prereqRationale: organized_priesthood: priests order the gods. cuneiform OR hieroglyphic: the god lists are written. All are earlier than ~2,600 BCE.
newNodes.rationale: organized_priesthood: priests order the gods. cuneiform OR hieroglyphic: the god lists are written. All are earlier than ~2,600 BCE.
newNodes.desc: The city gods are arranged in one ranked family under a high god, whose shrine confers kingship over all the cities.
newNodes.effectRationale: Conquered cities keep their gods inside the victor's pantheon and accept rule confirmed at the high god's shrine, so authority extends further.
newNodes.distinctFrom: organized_priesthood serves one city's god; this joins many cities' gods into one hierarchy that legitimizes rule over all of them.

newNodes.name: Temple relief
newNodes.emerged: ~2,400 BCE Lagash reforms protecting widows and orphans; ~2,100 BCE Ur III temple ration lists for dependants
newNodes.prereqRationale: temple_economy: the temple's stores and ration system feed the dependants (dated ~3,200 BCE).
newNodes.rationale: temple_economy: the temple's stores and ration system feed the dependants (dated ~3,200 BCE).
newNodes.desc: Temples put widows, orphans and the destitute on their ration lists in return for light work, so the weakest are fed from temple stores.
newNodes.effectRationale: Orphans and children of the destitute on temple rations are protected when harvests fail.
newNodes.distinctFrom: temple_economy is the estate management; this is the temple's relief role. debt_remission is a royal edict cancelling debts.

newNodes.name: Overkingship
newNodes.emerged: ~2,400 BCE Ebla's sworn overlordship of Abarsal; ~1,350 BCE Hittite vassal treaties
newNodes.prereqRationale: sacral_kingship: the overlord is a sanctioned king. sworn_treaties: vassal kings are bound by treaty oaths (Ebla-Abarsal, ~2,400 BCE, same date).
newNodes.rationale: sacral_kingship: the overlord is a sanctioned king. sworn_treaties: vassal kings are bound by treaty oaths (Ebla-Abarsal, ~2,400 BCE, same date).
newNodes.desc: A great king rules other kings, who keep their thrones in return for oaths, tribute and troops.
newNodes.effectRationale: Vassal tribute adds to what the overlord extracts without his own officials.
newNodes.distinctFrom: territorial_kingship rules directly through officials; overkingship rules indirectly through sworn sub-kings.

newNodes.name: Succession oaths
newNodes.emerged: 672 BCE Esarhaddon's succession treaties binding vassals and officials to Ashurbanipal
newNodes.prereqRationale: succession_law: the heir is named by rule. sworn_treaties: officials and vassals swear treaty oaths to uphold him. Both are A3 and earlier.
newNodes.rationale: succession_law: the heir is named by rule. sworn_treaties: officials and vassals swear treaty oaths to uphold him. Both are A3 and earlier.
newNodes.desc: Officials and vassal kings swear in the old ruler's lifetime to support his chosen heir, under curses if they break the oath.
newNodes.effectRationale: Governors sworn personally to the heir keep distant provinces loyal through the change of reign.
newNodes.distinctFrom: succession_law names the heir; these oaths bind the realm's officials to him before the accession.

newNodes.name: Ethical religion
newNodes.emerged: ~750 BCE Amos and the Hebrew prophets; ~600 BCE Zoroastrian teaching (dates debated)
newNodes.prereqRationale: organized_priesthood: the cult the prophets reform. law_code: divine justice is framed as law. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: organized_priesthood: the cult the prophets reform. law_code: divine justice is framed as law. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: Prophets teach that the gods demand justice for the poor rather than sacrifice alone, and judge kings and the rich by that standard.
newNodes.effectRationale: Religious duties of charity and fair dealing, and prophetic rebuke of the powerful, ease the grievances of the poor.
newNodes.distinctFrom: organized_priesthood is the cult; this is the moral content that holds rulers and rich to account. scriptural_canon fixes texts.

newNodes.name: Pilgrimage and sacred truce
newNodes.emerged: ~776 BCE Olympic sacred truce (ekecheiria); ~700 BCE pilgrims to the oracle at Delphi
newNodes.prereqRationale: organized_priesthood: sanctuaries are run by priests. track_road: pilgrims travel built routes. Both are much earlier.
newNodes.rationale: organized_priesthood: sanctuaries are run by priests. track_road: pilgrims travel built routes. Both are much earlier.
newNodes.desc: Sanctuaries draw pilgrims from many states; a sacred truce protects travellers on the roads to the festival.
newNodes.effectRationale: Safe passage under the truce and sanctuary hostels on the sacred ways let travellers cover more ground each day.
newNodes.distinctFrom: public_games is the contest; pilgrimage is the protected journey and the sanctuary network.

newNodes.name: Tyranny
newNodes.emerged: ~657 BCE Cypselus at Corinth; ~546 BCE Peisistratus at Athens
newNodes.prereqRationale: elite_council: tyrants rose from aristocratic faction struggles (~700 BCE). citizen_militia OR standing_army: hoplite backing or a bodyguard/mercenary force.
newNodes.rationale: elite_council: tyrants rose from aristocratic faction struggles (~700 BCE). citizen_militia OR standing_army: hoplite backing or a bodyguard/mercenary force.
newNodes.desc: A strongman seizes a city outside the traditional order, backed by the people or hired troops, and rules through patronage and public works.
newNodes.effectRationale: Tyrants employed the poor on public works (the Eupalinos tunnel, Peisistratid fountain-houses and roads), so more labour goes into building.
newNodes.distinctFrom: military_rule is government by the armed forces as a body; tyranny is one man's rule over a city, outside law but often popular.

newNodes.name: Ruler cult
newNodes.emerged: ~300 BCE Hellenistic ruler cults; 29 BCE first provincial temples to Augustus
newNodes.prereqRationale: sacral_kingship: the ruler is divine or god-sanctioned. provincial_administration: the cult is organized province by province.
newNodes.rationale: sacral_kingship: the ruler is divine or god-sanctioned. provincial_administration: the cult is organized province by province.
newNodes.desc: Provinces raise temples and priests to the living or deified ruler; local notables compete to hold the priesthood, binding them to the empire.
newNodes.effectRationale: Provincial elites who serve as the ruler's priests tie distant provinces to the centre, so authority reaches further.
newNodes.distinctFrom: sacral_kingship is the king's sanction by the gods; the ruler cult makes him an object of provincial worship run by local elites.

newNodes.name: Adoptive succession
newNodes.emerged: 96–180 CE Nerva–Antonine adoptive emperors
newNodes.prereqRationale: succession_law: succession by rule. family_law: adoption is a legal act of family law. Both are A3.
newNodes.rationale: succession_law: succession by rule. family_law: adoption is a legal act of family law. Both are A3.
newNodes.desc: The ruler adopts the ablest candidate as his son and heir, giving merit the form of dynastic succession.
newNodes.effectRationale: An heir chosen and designated in advance avoids contested accessions (the five good emperors), so unrest costs less output.
newNodes.distinctFrom: succession_law fixes the heir by birth order; adoption chooses him by ability while keeping dynastic form.

newNodes.name: Congregations
newNodes.emerged: ~250 BCE synagogue inscriptions in Egypt; ~50 CE Christian assemblies; Buddhist lay observance days
newNodes.prereqRationale: scriptural_canon: the congregation gathers to hear the text read. communal_feasts: the common meal of the assembly. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: scriptural_canon: the congregation gathers to hear the text read. communal_feasts: the common meal of the assembly. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: Lay believers meet weekly to hear scripture, share a meal and support their poor, sick and widows from a common fund.
newNodes.effectRationale: Congregational alms and shared meals keep members alive through dearth.
newNodes.distinctFrom: organized_priesthood and temple_almsgiving are run by priests; congregations are lay communities supporting their own members.

newNodes.name: State orthodoxy
newNodes.emerged: 136 BCE Han erudites of the Five Classics; 124 BCE Imperial Academy
newNodes.prereqRationale: mandate_doctrine: the Zhou doctrine is the core of Confucian legitimacy. philosophical_schools: one school is chosen as orthodox. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: mandate_doctrine: the Zhou doctrine is the core of Confucian legitimacy. philosophical_schools: one school is chosen as orthodox. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: One school of thought is made the state's official doctrine: its classics are taught at a state academy and mastery of them leads to office.
newNodes.effectRationale: Mastery of the official classics opens a route to office for men outside the old nobility.
newNodes.distinctFrom: state_religion establishes a faith and clergy; state orthodoxy establishes a doctrine and a curriculum for officials.

newNodes.name: Pious endowments
newNodes.emerged: ~700 CE early waqf foundations; ~980 CE Adudi hospital in Baghdad
newNodes.prereqRationale: state_religion: endowments are protected by the religious establishment. legal_code_roman: a perpetual trust needs a systematic law of property.
newNodes.rationale: state_religion: endowments are protected by the religious establishment. legal_code_roman: a perpetual trust needs a systematic law of property.
newNodes.desc: Land and shops are endowed in perpetuity to fund hospitals, fountains, schools and kitchens, managed by trustees under religious law.
newNodes.effectRationale: Hospitals, public fountains and soup kitchens funded in perpetuity lower baseline mortality.
newNodes.distinctFrom: temple_almsgiving is relief from temple stores; endowments are perpetual legal trusts with their own income.

newNodes.name: Church-state concordat
newNodes.emerged: 1107 CE Concordat of London; 1122 CE Concordat of Worms
newNodes.prereqRationale: state_religion: an established church. service_tenure: bishops hold lands as fiefs, which is what made investiture contested. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: state_religion: an established church. service_tenure: bishops hold lands as fiefs, which is what made investiture contested. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: Church and crown divide authority over bishops: the church confers spiritual office, the ruler the lands, ending wars over who appoints them.
newNodes.effectRationale: Settled jurisdiction ends the civil wars of the investiture conflict, so unrest costs less output.
newNodes.distinctFrom: state_religion makes the church official; the concordat sets the boundary between church and crown.

newNodes.name: Mendicant friars
newNodes.emerged: 1209 CE Franciscan rule; 1216 CE Dominican order
newNodes.prereqRationale: monasticism: friars live under a rule. canon_law: the papacy approved and regulated their orders (Gratian ~1,140 CE precedes 1209).
newNodes.rationale: monasticism: friars live under a rule. canon_law: the papacy approved and regulated their orders (Gratian ~1,140 CE precedes 1209).
newNodes.desc: Friars without property preach and beg in the towns, nursing the sick and serving the urban poor.
newNodes.effectRationale: Preaching and care among the urban poor ease grievance in growing towns.
newNodes.distinctFrom: monasticism withdraws from the world to estates; friars live among townspeople without estates.

newNodes.name: Holy war
newNodes.emerged: ~750 CE jihad doctrine in early Islamic law; 1095 CE First Crusade preached
newNodes.prereqRationale: state_religion: the faith sanctioning the war is established. standing_army: there are permanent forces to send. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: state_religion: the faith sanctioning the war is established. standing_army: there are permanent forces to send. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: War against unbelievers is declared a religious duty with spiritual rewards, and conquered frontier land is settled by the faithful.
newNodes.effectRationale: Frontier land granted to settlers under holy war (Reconquista repopulation, crusader states) draws migrants over long distances.
newNodes.distinctFrom: military_orders are the fighting monks; this is the doctrine that sanctions the war and the settlement behind it.

newNodes.name: Primogeniture
newNodes.emerged: ~1,000 CE Capetian succession of eldest sons; ~1,100 CE indivisible fiefs in Normandy and England
newNodes.prereqRationale: succession_law: the rule of inheritance. service_tenure: fiefs held for service must not be divided. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: succession_law: the rule of inheritance. service_tenure: fiefs held for service must not be divided. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: The eldest son inherits the realm or fief undivided; younger sons go to the church, the army or abroad.
newNodes.effectRationale: Realms are no longer partitioned among sons (Carolingian partitions against Capetian continuity), so authority holds over the whole territory.
newNodes.distinctFrom: succession_law names an heir; primogeniture also keeps the inheritance undivided.

newNodes.name: Caliphate
newNodes.emerged: 632 CE Rashidun caliphate; 750 CE Abbasid caliphate
newNodes.prereqRationale: scriptural_canon: the caliph rules a community defined by scripture. state_religion: the faith is established. provincial_administration: the caliphate governed by provinces and a fiscal register.
newNodes.rationale: scriptural_canon: the caliph rules a community defined by scripture. state_religion: the faith is established. provincial_administration: the caliphate governed by provinces and a fiscal register.
newNodes.desc: The successor of the Prophet leads the community of believers in war, law and taxation, through governors and a register of revenues.
newNodes.effectRationale: The land tax, poll tax on non-Muslims and the diwan register raised extraction across the provinces.
newNodes.distinctFrom: theocracy is rule by priests under religious law; the caliph is a lay successor-ruler, not a priest.

newNodes.name: Confessional state
newNodes.emerged: 1555 CE Peace of Augsburg; 1563 CE Tridentine parish registers
newNodes.prereqRationale: religious_reform: there are rival confessions to choose between (1517). state_religion: the ruler's church is established.
newNodes.rationale: religious_reform: there are rival confessions to choose between (1517). state_religion: the ruler's church is established.
newNodes.desc: Each ruler fixes his territory's confession; the church keeps parish registers of births, marriages and deaths and disciplines the parish.
newNodes.effectRationale: Parish registers and church discipline give the state eyes in every parish, extending administrative reach.
newNodes.distinctFrom: state_religion establishes a faith; confessionalization builds parish registration and discipline in each territory's confession.

newNodes.name: Revival movements
newNodes.emerged: ~1,690 CE German Pietism and the Halle foundations; ~1,735 CE Great Awakening
newNodes.prereqRationale: religious_reform: revival builds on lay reading of scripture (1517).
newNodes.rationale: religious_reform: revival builds on lay reading of scripture (1517).
newNodes.desc: Lay devotional circles call for personal conversion and good works, founding orphanages, charity schools and Bible societies.
newNodes.effectRationale: Orphanages and charity schools (Halle) protect poor children in dearth.
newNodes.distinctFrom: religious_reform founds new churches; revivalism renews piety inside them and builds charitable foundations.

newNodes.name: Reason of state
newNodes.emerged: 1589 CE Botero, Della ragion di stato; ~1,630 CE Richelieu's policy
newNodes.prereqRationale: statecraft_doctrine: the ancient doctrine of state interest. printing_press: the doctrine spread in print. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: statecraft_doctrine: the ancient doctrine of state interest. printing_press: the doctrine spread in print. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: The interest of the state is placed above religious and dynastic claims: rulers build revenue, armies and alliances for the state's sake.
newNodes.effectRationale: The fiscal-military state organizes revenue for its own sake, so it extracts more.
newNodes.distinctFrom: statecraft_doctrine is advice to rulers; reason of state elevates the state's interest above faith and dynasty.

newNodes.name: Plebiscitary legitimacy
newNodes.emerged: 1799–1804 CE Napoleonic plebiscites; 1851–1852 CE plebiscites of Louis-Napoleon
newNodes.prereqRationale: popular_sovereignty: the people is the source of authority (1776). census: a register of voters is needed.
newNodes.rationale: popular_sovereignty: the people is the source of authority (1776). census: a register of voters is needed.
newNodes.desc: A ruler seeks the people's direct approval in a yes-or-no vote on his rule or constitution, bypassing representatives.
newNodes.effectRationale: A ruler with a popular mandate faces less open resistance, so unrest costs less output.
newNodes.distinctFrom: referendum lets citizens decide a law; a plebiscite asks them to endorse a ruler or regime.

newNodes.name: Civic ritual
newNodes.emerged: 1790 CE Fête de la Fédération; 1795 CE La Marseillaise adopted; 1880 CE Bastille Day
newNodes.prereqRationale: popular_sovereignty: the nation honoured is the sovereign people. public_games: civic festivals continue public festival practice. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: popular_sovereignty: the nation honoured is the sovereign people. public_games: civic festivals continue public festival practice. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: Flags, anthems, national holidays and monuments give the sovereign nation its own rites, celebrated in every town.
newNodes.effectRationale: National symbols and festivals reach every commune, so the state's authority is recognized further from the capital.
newNodes.distinctFrom: nationalism is the doctrine; civic ritual is its calendar of festivals and symbols.

newNodes.name: Social Christianity
newNodes.emerged: 1848 CE Christian socialists in London; ~1,880 CE Social Gospel; 1891 CE Rerum Novarum
newNodes.prereqRationale: labour_unions: churches respond to the labour question (1824). state_religion: the established churches take up the cause.
newNodes.rationale: labour_unions: churches respond to the labour question (1824). state_religion: the established churches take up the cause.
newNodes.desc: Churches take up the labour question, backing fair wages, workers' associations, settlement houses and relief for the industrial poor.
newNodes.effectRationale: Church-backed relief and arbitration ease industrial grievance.
newNodes.distinctFrom: socialism demands collective ownership; social Christianity seeks reform within property and church.

newNodes.name: Missionary societies
newNodes.emerged: 1792 CE Baptist Missionary Society; 1795 CE London Missionary Society
newNodes.prereqRationale: missionary_religion: the duty to convert. printing_press: subscription societies print and distribute scripture and reports.
newNodes.rationale: missionary_religion: the duty to convert. printing_press: subscription societies print and distribute scripture and reports.
newNodes.desc: Voluntary societies fund missionaries abroad, who found schools and clinics and send home reports and maps of the interior.
newNodes.effectRationale: Missionary travellers (Livingstone) mapped interiors unknown to outsiders, so each exploration reaches further.
newNodes.distinctFrom: missionary_religion is the duty to convert; these are the organized, subscription-funded overseas societies.

newNodes.name: Plebiscitary empire
newNodes.emerged: 1804 CE First French Empire by plebiscite; 1852 CE Second Empire
newNodes.prereqRationale: plebiscite: the regime is legitimized by popular vote (1799). universal_conscription: it rests on a mass army (1793).
newNodes.rationale: plebiscite: the regime is legitimized by popular vote (1799). universal_conscription: it rests on a mass army (1793).
newNodes.desc: An emperor rules with authoritarian powers confirmed by plebiscites, through prefects, a mass army and public works.
newNodes.effectRationale: Prefects appointed from the capital govern every department, extending administrative reach.
newNodes.distinctFrom: absolute_monarchy rests on dynastic right; this form rests on plebiscites and the mass army.

newNodes.name: Feminism
newNodes.emerged: 1792 CE A Vindication of the Rights of Woman; 1848 CE Seneca Falls Declaration
newNodes.prereqRationale: social_contract: equal natural rights are claimed for women (Wollstonecraft answered Rousseau).
newNodes.rationale: social_contract: equal natural rights are claimed for women (Wollstonecraft answered Rousseau).
newNodes.desc: A movement claims for women the rights of citizens: education, property, the professions and the vote.
newNodes.effectRationale: Opening education and professions to women enlarges the pool for specialist classes.
newNodes.distinctFrom: womens_suffrage is the vote; feminism is the wider movement for education, property and work.

newNodes.name: Social democracy
newNodes.emerged: 1875 CE Gotha programme; 1891 CE Erfurt programme; 1899 CE Bernstein's revisionism
newNodes.prereqRationale: socialism: the goal. mass_political_party: the party organization. mass_suffrage: the electoral route. All are earlier than 1875.
newNodes.rationale: socialism: the goal. mass_political_party: the party organization. mass_suffrage: the electoral route. All are earlier than 1875.
newNodes.desc: Socialist parties seek reform through elections and parliament: social insurance, labour law and public services instead of revolution.
newNodes.effectRationale: Strikes and protest are channelled into parliamentary bargaining, so unrest costs less output.
newNodes.distinctFrom: socialism is the movement's goal; social democracy is its parliamentary, reformist strategy.

newNodes.name: New imperialism
newNodes.emerged: ~1,870 CE civilizing-mission doctrine; 1884–1885 CE Berlin Conference
newNodes.prereqRationale: nationalism: empire as national prestige. colonial_administration: the apparatus to rule colonies. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: nationalism: empire as national prestige. colonial_administration: the apparatus to rule colonies. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: Overseas empire is argued to be a national necessity and a civilizing mission; colonies are claimed and settled by agreement among powers.
newNodes.effectRationale: State-sponsored emigration and settlement schemes send larger founding parties.
newNodes.distinctFrom: colonial_administration governs colonies; this is the doctrine that drives their acquisition.

newNodes.name: Progressivism
newNodes.emerged: ~1,890 CE US Progressive movement; 1906 CE Pure Food and Drug Act
newNodes.prereqRationale: classical_liberalism: progressives reformed liberal capitalism. mass_press: muckraking journalism drove reform. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: classical_liberalism: progressives reformed liberal capitalism. mass_press: muckraking journalism drove reform. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: Reformers use investigative journalism, experts and regulation to clean up cities, food, factories and politics.
newNodes.effectRationale: Pure-food laws, sanitary reform and municipal clean-up lower baseline mortality.
newNodes.distinctFrom: classical_liberalism limits government; progressivism uses it to regulate.

newNodes.name: Semi-presidential republic
newNodes.emerged: 1919 CE Weimar constitution; 1958 CE French Fifth Republic
newNodes.prereqRationale: ministerial_responsibility: the cabinet answers to parliament. separation_of_powers: a separately elected president. mass_suffrage: both are popularly elected.
newNodes.rationale: ministerial_responsibility: the cabinet answers to parliament. separation_of_powers: a separately elected president. mass_suffrage: both are popularly elected.
newNodes.desc: A directly elected president shares executive power with a prime minister responsible to parliament.
newNodes.effectRationale: A president able to dissolve parliament and appoint governments ends chronic cabinet crises (the Fourth Republic), so disorder costs less output.
newNodes.distinctFrom: presidential_republic has no prime minister responsible to parliament; parliamentary_government has no elected president with real powers.

newNodes.name: Dominant-party system
newNodes.emerged: 1929 CE Mexico's National Revolutionary Party; 1955 CE Japan's Liberal Democratic Party
newNodes.prereqRationale: mass_political_party: the dominant party. mass_suffrage: elections are held and won. Both are 19th century.
newNodes.rationale: mass_political_party: the dominant party. mass_suffrage: elections are held and won. Both are 19th century.
newNodes.desc: One party wins every election for decades while opposition parties remain legal; politics happens among its factions.
newNodes.effectRationale: Factions inside the governing party bargain over demands, absorbing grievance.
newNodes.distinctFrom: one_party_state bans other parties; here opposition is legal but never wins.

newNodes.name: Personalist dictatorship
newNodes.emerged: 1930 CE Trujillo in the Dominican Republic; 1965 CE Mobutu in Zaire
newNodes.prereqRationale: personality_cult: the ruler's cult (1929). standing_army: the force that keeps him in power.
newNodes.rationale: personality_cult: the ruler's cult (1929). standing_army: the force that keeps him in power.
newNodes.desc: One man rules through family, cronies and a loyal guard, above any party or army institution.
newNodes.effectRationale: The ruler's network extracts revenue from monopolies and concessions directly, raising extraction.
newNodes.distinctFrom: military_rule is rule by the army as a body; one_party_state by a party; here power is personal.

newNodes.name: Clerical republic
newNodes.emerged: 1979 CE Islamic Republic of Iran
newNodes.prereqRationale: religious_political_movements: the movement that takes power (1928). written_constitution and mass_suffrage: an elected parliament and president under a constitution.
newNodes.rationale: religious_political_movements: the movement that takes power (1928). written_constitution and mass_suffrage: an elected parliament and president under a constitution.
newNodes.desc: Elected institutions govern under the guardianship of senior clerics, who can veto laws and candidates.
newNodes.effectRationale: Revolutionary construction foundations built rural roads cheaply with volunteer labour (Construction Jihad, 1979), so paths cost less to build.
newNodes.distinctFrom: theocracy is government by religious office; here elected republican institutions sit under clerical guardianship.

newNodes.name: Supranational union
newNodes.emerged: 1951 CE European Coal and Steel Community; 1993 CE European Union
newNodes.prereqRationale: customs_union: the common market's base (1834). international_organizations: permanent treaty bodies (1865).
newNodes.rationale: customs_union: the common market's base (1834). international_organizations: permanent treaty bodies (1865).
newNodes.desc: Member states pool sovereignty in common institutions with their own law, court and market, and allow free movement of goods and people.
newNodes.effectRationale: A single market closes price gaps and free movement lets people relocate across member states.
newNodes.distinctFrom: federal_republic is one sovereign state; a supranational union pools only part of its members' sovereignty.

newNodes.name: Cult of personality
newNodes.emerged: 1929 CE Stalin's fiftieth-birthday campaign; 1966 CE Mao's Little Red Book campaigns
newNodes.prereqRationale: state_propaganda: the cult is built by propaganda (1917). mass_political_party: the party venerates its leader.
newNodes.rationale: state_propaganda: the cult is built by propaganda (1917). mass_political_party: the party venerates its leader.
newNodes.desc: The leader is glorified as infallible in portraits, songs and slogans; loyalty to him becomes the test of loyalty to the state.
newNodes.effectRationale: The leader's image and directives reach every village and workplace, extending administrative reach.
newNodes.distinctFrom: state_propaganda is a ministry and method; the cult concentrates legitimacy in one person.

newNodes.name: Constitutional court
newNodes.emerged: 1920 CE Austrian Constitutional Court (Kelsen); 1951 CE German Federal Constitutional Court
newNodes.prereqRationale: judicial_review: courts may void laws (1803). written_constitution: the court guards a written text.
newNodes.rationale: judicial_review: courts may void laws (1803). written_constitution: the court guards a written text.
newNodes.desc: A special court rules on whether laws and official acts are constitutional and settles disputes between branches and levels of government.
newNodes.effectRationale: Disputes over power are settled in court instead of the street, and federal law applies uniformly across regions.
newNodes.distinctFrom: judicial_review is any court's power to void laws; this is a dedicated court that arbitrates the constitution itself.

newNodes.name: Transitional justice
newNodes.emerged: 1983 CE Argentine truth commission (CONADEP); 1995 CE South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission
newNodes.prereqRationale: human_rights: the standard abuses are judged by (1948). international_tribunals: the precedent of trying a fallen regime (1945).
newNodes.rationale: human_rights: the standard abuses are judged by (1948). international_tribunals: the precedent of trying a fallen regime (1945).
newNodes.desc: After a dictatorship or civil war, truth commissions, trials and reparations establish what happened and give the new order legitimacy.
newNodes.effectRationale: Acknowledgment and reparations for past abuses ease the grievances of victims.
newNodes.distinctFrom: international_tribunals try individuals; transitional justice is the domestic process that legitimizes a new regime.

newNodes.name: Power-sharing
newNodes.emerged: 1943 CE Lebanese National Pact; 1998 CE Good Friday Agreement
newNodes.prereqRationale: mass_suffrage: each community is represented by vote. religious_toleration: communities of different faiths accept one another. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: mass_suffrage: each community is represented by vote. religious_toleration: communities of different faiths accept one another. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: Offices, seats and vetoes are divided among a country's communities by agreement, so no group can rule the others alone.
newNodes.effectRationale: Each community holds a guaranteed share and veto, which eases grievance and reduces violent disorder.
newNodes.distinctFrom: federal_republic divides power by territory; power-sharing divides it among communities.

newNodes.name: Term limits
newNodes.emerged: 1917 CE Mexican no-reelection clause; 1951 CE US Twenty-second Amendment
newNodes.prereqRationale: separation_of_powers: an elected executive to limit. mass_suffrage: the electorate whose choices term limits renew.
newNodes.rationale: separation_of_powers: an elected executive to limit. mass_suffrage: the electorate whose choices term limits renew.
newNodes.desc: The head of government may serve only a fixed number of terms, forcing regular turnover at the top.
newNodes.effectRationale: Forced turnover opens top offices to new people.
newNodes.distinctFrom: presidential_republic fixes terms; term limits cap how many a person may hold.

newNodes.name: Independent electoral administration
newNodes.emerged: 1920 CE Canada's Chief Electoral Officer; 1950 CE Election Commission of India
newNodes.prereqRationale: secret_ballot: the vote to protect (1856). merit_civil_service: non-partisan officials to run it (1854).
newNodes.rationale: secret_ballot: the vote to protect (1856). merit_civil_service: non-partisan officials to run it (1854).
newNodes.desc: Elections are run by an independent body of officials, not by the government in power, so results are trusted by losers.
newNodes.effectRationale: Citizens who regard the government as fairly chosen comply with taxes more readily.
newNodes.distinctFrom: secret_ballot protects the voter; this protects the count and the electoral roll.

newNodes.name: Ceremonial monarchy
newNodes.emerged: 1947 CE Japanese constitution's symbolic emperor; 1974 CE Swedish Instrument of Government
newNodes.prereqRationale: succession_law: the throne remains hereditary. ministerial_responsibility and mass_suffrage: elected ministers hold all real power.
newNodes.rationale: succession_law: the throne remains hereditary. ministerial_responsibility and mass_suffrage: elected ministers hold all real power.
newNodes.desc: The hereditary monarch keeps only ceremonial duties as a non-partisan symbol of the state, above party politics.
newNodes.effectRationale: A non-partisan head of state can arbitrate constitutional crises (Spain 1981), so disorder costs less output.
newNodes.distinctFrom: constitutional_monarchy still gives the monarch political powers; here the role is purely symbolic.

newNodes.name: Ecumenical movement
newNodes.emerged: 1910 CE Edinburgh Missionary Conference; 1948 CE World Council of Churches; 1965 CE Nostra aetate
newNodes.prereqRationale: religious_toleration: churches accept one another. international_organizations: the World Council of Churches is a permanent international body.
newNodes.rationale: religious_toleration: churches accept one another. international_organizations: the World Council of Churches is a permanent international body.
newNodes.desc: Churches and faiths cooperate through councils and dialogue instead of competing for converts and condemning one another.
newNodes.effectRationale: Cooperation among confessions reduces sectarian conflict.
newNodes.distinctFrom: religious_toleration is state policy; ecumenism is cooperation among the faiths themselves.

newNodes.name: Liberation theology
newNodes.emerged: 1968 CE Medellín bishops' conference; 1971 CE Gutiérrez, A Theology of Liberation
newNodes.prereqRationale: systematic_theology: a theological method. socialism: its social analysis. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: systematic_theology: a theological method. socialism: its social analysis. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: Clergy and lay base communities read scripture as a call to free the poor, organizing cooperatives, soup kitchens and land claims.
newNodes.effectRationale: Base communities run communal kitchens and mutual aid, so households absorb food shortfalls.
newNodes.distinctFrom: social_christianity is reform from above; liberation theology organizes the poor themselves.

newNodes.name: Religious mass movements
newNodes.emerged: 1925 CE Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh; 1928 CE Muslim Brotherhood; ~1,945 CE Christian Democratic parties
newNodes.prereqRationale: mass_political_party: the mass-membership organization. scriptural_canon: the religious programme. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: mass_political_party: the mass-membership organization. scriptural_canon: the religious programme. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: Mass movements seek to order state and society by religious values, combining preaching, welfare networks and electoral politics.
newNodes.effectRationale: Their welfare networks feed members and neighbours in hard times.
newNodes.distinctFrom: state_religion is establishment by a ruler; these are mass movements from below.

newNodes.name: Religious relief agencies
newNodes.emerged: 1942 CE Oxfam (Quaker-founded); 1943 CE Catholic Relief Services
newNodes.prereqRationale: social_christianity: relief as religious duty. international_organizations: the agencies work across borders. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: social_christianity: relief as religious duty. international_organizations: the agencies work across borders. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: Religious agencies run famine relief, child feeding and refugee aid across borders.
newNodes.effectRationale: Child-feeding programmes protect children in famine.
newNodes.distinctFrom: temple_almsgiving is local; these are international agencies with supply chains.

newNodes.name: Vanguard party
newNodes.emerged: 1902 CE What Is to Be Done? (doctrine); 1917 CE Bolshevik seizure of power
newNodes.prereqRationale: socialism: the goal. mass_political_party: the party form, remade as a disciplined vanguard. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: socialism: the goal. mass_political_party: the party form, remade as a disciplined vanguard. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: A disciplined party of professional revolutionaries claims to lead the working class, seize power and run the state in its name.
newNodes.effectRationale: Party cadres promote workers and peasants into management and office.
newNodes.distinctFrom: socialism is the movement; the vanguard party is its Leninist organization for taking power.

newNodes.name: Nonviolent resistance
newNodes.emerged: 1919 CE satyagraha against the Rowlatt Acts; 1930 CE Salt March; 1955 CE Montgomery bus boycott
newNodes.prereqRationale: mass_press: public opinion is the lever. mass_political_party: mass organization. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: mass_press: public opinion is the lever. mass_political_party: mass organization. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: Movements break unjust laws openly and without violence, using boycotts, strikes and marches to win public opinion.
newNodes.effectRationale: Protest that refuses violence costs far less output than riot or insurrection.
newNodes.distinctFrom: civil_rights_law is the legal result; nonviolent resistance is the method that won it.

newNodes.name: Neoliberalism
newNodes.emerged: 1947 CE Mont Pèlerin Society; 1979–1980 CE deregulation in Britain and the United States
newNodes.prereqRationale: classical_liberalism: free-market tradition. central_banking: monetarist policy works through the central bank. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: classical_liberalism: free-market tradition. central_banking: monetarist policy works through the central bank. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: Markets are promoted over state management: privatization, deregulation, independent central banks and open capital flows.
newNodes.effectRationale: Deregulation of freight (trucking, rail and shipping, 1980) cut haulage costs.
newNodes.distinctFrom: classical_liberalism argued against mercantilism; neoliberalism against the post-war mixed economy.

newNodes.name: Developmental state
newNodes.emerged: 1949 CE Japan's MITI; ~1,950 CE ECLA import-substitution doctrine; 1961 CE South Korean Economic Planning Board
newNodes.prereqRationale: central_planning: plans and targets. nationalism: development as national goal. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: central_planning: plans and targets. nationalism: development as national goal. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: The state guides private industry with credit, targets and protection to catch up with industrial nations.
newNodes.effectRationale: State-led industrialization and technical schooling enlarge the skilled and specialist classes.
newNodes.distinctFrom: central_planning replaces markets; the developmental state steers private firms within them.

newNodes.name: Multiculturalism
newNodes.emerged: 1971 CE Canadian multiculturalism policy; 1975 CE Swedish immigrant policy
newNodes.prereqRationale: secular_state: equality of faiths. human_rights: equal dignity of all residents. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: secular_state: equality of faiths. human_rights: equal dignity of all residents. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: The state recognizes and supports the cultures of immigrant and minority communities as part of the nation.
newNodes.effectRationale: Recognition and settlement support make immigration easier, so people move more freely.
newNodes.distinctFrom: secular_state treats faiths equally; multiculturalism supports distinct communities' cultures.

newNodes.name: Environmentalism
newNodes.emerged: 1962 CE Silent Spring; 1970 CE first Earth Day; 1980 CE West German Greens
newNodes.prereqRationale: nature_conservation: protection of nature (1872). mass_press: public campaigns drove the movement. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: nature_conservation: protection of nature (1872). mass_press: public campaigns drove the movement. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: A mass movement demands protection of air, water, land and climate, and green parties enter parliaments.
newNodes.effectRationale: Campaigns against pollution and toxic chemicals lower baseline mortality.
newNodes.distinctFrom: environmental_regulation is the law; environmentalism is the movement that demands it.

newNodes.name: Mass populism
newNodes.emerged: 1930 CE Vargas in Brazil; 1946 CE Perón in Argentina
newNodes.prereqRationale: mass_suffrage: populists win elections. labour_unions: they incorporate the unions. nationalism: they speak for the nation. All are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: mass_suffrage: populists win elections. labour_unions: they incorporate the unions. nationalism: they speak for the nation. All are earlier.
newNodes.desc: A leader claims to speak for the common people against the elite, winning elections and bringing unions under the state.
newNodes.effectRationale: Wage gains and recognition for organized workers ease grievance.
newNodes.distinctFrom: fascism abolishes elections; populism wins them and keeps them.

newNodes.name: Modernizing nationalism
newNodes.emerged: 1923–1938 CE Atatürk's reforms; 1928 CE Turkish alphabet reform
newNodes.prereqRationale: nationalism: the national programme. secular_state: separation of religion and state. compulsory_education: mass schooling. All are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: nationalism: the national programme. secular_state: separation of religion and state. compulsory_education: mass schooling. All are earlier.
newNodes.desc: A nationalist state modernizes by decree: secular law, script reform, Western dress and mass schooling.
newNodes.effectRationale: Script reform and literacy campaigns spread learning, so more people contribute to civic knowledge.
newNodes.distinctFrom: nationalism defines the nation; this programme remakes its society from above.

newNodes.name: Social liberalism
newNodes.emerged: 1933–1935 CE New Deal; 1942 CE Beveridge Report
newNodes.prereqRationale: classical_liberalism: the liberal tradition. income_tax: funds social insurance. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: classical_liberalism: the liberal tradition. income_tax: funds social insurance. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: Liberals accept that the state must insure citizens against unemployment, sickness and old age to keep a free society.
newNodes.effectRationale: Unemployment and old-age insurance let households ride out lost income.
newNodes.distinctFrom: classical_liberalism limits the state; social liberalism adds social insurance.

newNodes.name: Liberal internationalism
newNodes.emerged: 1918 CE Fourteen Points; 1945 CE United Nations Charter
newNodes.prereqRationale: classical_liberalism: free trade and rights. international_organizations: permanent international bodies. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: classical_liberalism: free trade and rights. international_organizations: permanent international bodies. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: Peace is to be kept by open trade, self-determination and international institutions.
newNodes.effectRationale: Lower tariffs and open sea lanes close price gaps between countries.
newNodes.distinctFrom: collective_security is the alliance mechanism; liberal internationalism is the doctrine behind it.

newNodes.name: Pan-national movements
newNodes.emerged: 1945 CE Fifth Pan-African Congress; 1945 CE Arab League; 1963 CE Organisation of African Unity
newNodes.prereqRationale: nationalism: the shared identity. international_organizations: regional bodies. Both are earlier.
newNodes.rationale: nationalism: the shared identity. international_organizations: regional bodies. Both are earlier.
newNodes.desc: Movements unite peoples across many states by shared language, history or continent, and found regional organizations.
newNodes.effectRationale: Regional free-movement agreements let people travel further.
newNodes.distinctFrom: nationalism builds one nation-state; pan-national movements unite many.

findings: Dependency changes proposed: 2. (1) marxist_leninist_state adds socialism: the A8 ideology was a leaf and the communist party-state could be founded without it, unlike fascist_state, which requires fascism; socialism (1825-1848) predates 1922. The edge lands only when D13 is imported, since socialism is a D13 civic and marxist_leninist_state is runtime. (2) religious_reform: printing_press AND (canon_law OR scriptural_canon) becomes printing_press AND scriptural_canon. The canon_law branch allowed reform without any scripture; canon_law keeps a dependent through the new mendicant_orders.

Leaves resolved by new nodes rather than new edges: ancestor_veneration feeds first_settler_rights and segmentary_lineage; mandate_doctrine feeds state_orthodoxy; systematic_theology feeds liberation_theology; missionary_religion feeds missionary_societies; secular_state feeds multiculturalism and modernizing_nationalism; socialism feeds social_democracy, vanguard_party and liberation_theology. The remaining leaves are deliberate: all regime forms (by rule), divine_right and conservatism (doctrines that are answered, not built on).

Regime-form rule: no new node requires a regime form. personalist_dictatorship needs personality_cult (an L node), clerical_republic needs religious_political_movements (a B node), and bonapartist_regime needs plebiscite (an L node), so the 'leaf' rule holds while each new form still has a distinct legitimacy source. Eleven new forms, each historically distinct from the existing 22: big_man_polity, segmentary_lineage (A2), overkingship (A3), tyranny (A4), caliphate (A6), bonapartist_regime (A8), semi_presidential_republic, dominant_party_system, personalist_dictatorship, clerical_republic, supranational_union (A9).

Operand pressure (group totals, before C2-C5): society.unrestOutputDrag 0.42 of cap 0.6 and society.grievanceRelief 0.31 of cap 0.6, while the technology groups already sum to 0.07 and 0.40 respectively. Combined with the other civics groups both operands will exceed their caps; the integrator should rescale them per tree (as T6 asked for research points) or raise the caps. This group routed most legitimacy and regime effects to governance.authorityDecayCostUnits (cap 3.0) and governance.taxExtractionResponseMax (cap 1.5) to limit the overflow. research.civicsPointsCoefficient is used only twice (0.04) because other groups already sum to 0.27 against 0.3.

Civ VII analogue correction: the D13 record gives conservatism the Civ VII analogue 'Absolutism', but in Civ VII Absolutism is the third node of the Fascism ideology branch (Military-Industrial Complex, Strategic Railways, Scorched Earth), not Burkean conservatism; the audit marks conservatism none-by-design. Civ VII's 'Divine Right' is a tradition in the Sovereignty civic (direct analogue for divine_right).

Emerged-text issues (no edge change): tribal_confederacy (A2) cites only 209 BCE and ~1450 CE; city_state_oligarchy (A3) cites ~700 BCE but Old Assyrian Assur (~1,900 BCE) supports A3; scriptural_canon's script prerequisite conflicts with the oral Rigveda in its emerged text. The integrator should amend these texts so the Age placements read as capability-based.

Redundant atoms kept (no closure change): printing_press in nationalism (social_contract already requires it) and mass_political_party in fascist_state (fascism requires it). They are harmless and document the print and party arguments.

Pacing: the A9 civics share grows the most (27 new legitimacy/belief/regime/ideology nodes), consistent with Civ VI/VII's dense modern-era political content (Civ VII Modern Age has three 3-node ideology branches plus Political Theory, Nationalism, Globalism, Hegemony). Per contract §5, A9 node costs should be scaled down per Age, not stacked; the factors here use the Age priors so the integrator's per-(tree, Age) scale applies directly.
